summary: TRILL routes frames through multi-hop networks with arbitrary topologies. This document extends its labeling of data packets beyond the base protocol's limit, so more separate groups of traffic can be told apart.

eli5.summary: In a big building with many mailrooms, each stack of mail needs a tag. This allows far more distinct tags.

questions: how many labels does trill fgl support
subtitle: How TRILL grows its data labels from about 4,000 VLAN IDs to 24-bit fine-grained labels for large data centers.

tldr.problem: The TRILL base protocol can label data packets with only up to 4K IDs, which is too few for large data centers with more than 4K users who each need configurable isolation.
tldr.mechanism: Fine-grained labeling (FGL) adds a 24-bit label, split into a 12-bit high part and a 12-bit low part, carried after the inner MAC addresses behind the Ethertype 0x893B. Special rules keep older VLAN-labeled RBridges from ever receiving FGL packets.
tldr.outcome: FGL provides 2**24 labels, far more than the 4094 VLAN labels of the base protocol. It is an optional extension that updates RFC 6325 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 7172 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6325; the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its fine-grained labeling is an optional extension to the TRILL base protocol.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs Bigger Labels
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links, RFC 6325) routes frames through multi-hop networks with arbitrary topologies, using IS-IS link-state routing and a hop count. TRILL switches are also called RBridges. The base protocol can label TRILL Data packets with up to 4K IDs.

Some applications need many more labels, for isolating tenants, service instances and the like. The RFC's first goal is blunt: the base labeling gives only 212 minus 2 valid identifiers (VLANs), and a substantially larger number is required. Fine-grained labeling (FGL) is the optional extension that provides it. It is mainly meant for large data centers with more than 4K users who need configurable data isolation from each other.

The RFC lists four goals in priority order: fine-grained labels, reuse of features that fast-path silicon already supports, interoperation with base RBridges, and an alternate priority for traffic crossing the TRILL network. The essence of FGL is that frames can carry a label from a far larger set, switch ports are labeled with sets of such labels, and an FGL packet cannot leave through a port unless its label matches one of the port's labels.
sections.eli5: The old system had only about four thousand label stickers, and a giant data center ran out. This RFC invents longer stickers so there are plenty for everyone.

sections.title: The FGL Label Format
sections.content:
In a base-protocol (VL, for VLAN Labeled) packet, the inner MAC addresses are followed by Ethertype 0x8100 and a 2-byte Inner.VLAN label that includes a 12-bit VLAN ID.

An FGL packet instead has 0x893B, then the Inner.Label High Part (2 bytes), then 0x893B again, then the Inner.Label Low Part (2 bytes). The two occurrences of 0x893B are mandatory: a switch that sees some other value in the second spot MUST discard the packet. The FGL is written (X.Y), where X is the 12-bit high part and Y the 12-bit low part.

In each 2-byte part the low 12 bits carry label information. The top 4 bits hold a 3-bit priority and a Drop Eligibility Indicator (DEI) bit. The priority in the High Part is the one used to carry the frame across the campus. The priority in the Low Part is remembered from the original frame and restored on egress.

Labels also differ in meaning. VL IDs mean the same thing everywhere in the campus and share a space with the C-VLAN IDs on Ethernet links. The FGL space is separate and flat, and each FGL port maps its native C-VLAN to an FGL on ingress and back on egress, possibly differently per port. The network manager is responsible for configuring these mappings.
sections.eli5: The new label has two halves, like a street name plus a house number. Each half also carries a small note about how important the mail is, so that note can be put back when the mail is delivered.

sections.title: Ingress, Transit and Egress
sections.content:
A switch recognizes an FGL packet by seeing 0x893B right after the Inner.MacSA. At the edge, ports can be configured to ingress native frames as FGL, by default through a per-port mapping from the frame's C-VLAN to an FGL. Ports not so configured keep doing ordinary VL ingress. Ingress MUST copy the frame's priority and DEI into the Inner.Label Low Part, and puts a mapped priority (or, if mapping is unsupported, the original) in the High Part.

Broadcast, multicast and unknown-destination frames can be handled two ways. They can go out as multi-destination packets on a distribution tree rooted at an FGL RBridge, and never on a tree rooted at a VL switch. Or they can be sent by serial unicast to each relevant egress switch. An ingress switch SHOULD use unicast if there is only one relevant egress FGL switch.

Transit switches forward unicast packets as usual and take priority and DEI from the same place in the packet for VL and FGL. For multi-destination packets, an FGL switch SHOULD prune the tree based on which branches advertise interest in label (X.Y). Pruning is only an optimization.

On egress, the switch converts the FGL back to a C-VLAN ID per port and takes priority and DEI from the Low Part. It MUST NOT egress an FGL packet with label (X.Y) to a port not configured with that FGL, even if the port carries VL packets in VLAN X. Address learning on FGL ports uses the label instead of the VLAN. Default tree-root priority for FGL nicknames is 0x9000, so FGL trees are preferred.
sections.eli5: When mail enters the building, a clerk swaps the old sticker for a new long one. Inside, the mail is only delivered to mailboxes with a matching sticker, and at the door the old sticker goes back on.

sections.title: Mixing FGL and VLAN-Only Switches
sections.content:
An RBridge that cannot safely transit FGL packets is a VL RBridge. A badly built one could egress an FGL packet into the wrong VLAN, persistently reorder it by miscomputing flows for ECMP, or prune its distribution wrongly. An FGL-safe switch is one that avoids all this and says so in its LSP. VL and FGL-safe switches coexist without disruption as long as no FGL packets are introduced, so the RFC advises upgrading VL switches before introducing FGL edges.

Once an FGL edge is advertised, an FGL-safe switch that sees a VL neighbor on a port MUST take Step A or Step B for that port, plus Step C.

  • Step A: if it can discard FGL packets on that port while still passing VL packets, it does so and raises the reported cost of adjacencies out of that port by 223 (capped at 224 minus 2), so paths through FGL-safe switches are preferred.
  • Step B: otherwise it reports those adjacencies at cost 224 minus 1, which keeps them out of least-cost path and tree calculations.
  • Step C: trees used for FGL data must be rooted at an FGL-safe switch or an FGL link pseudonode.

If links are slow (about 100 megabits/second or less) or costs are set non-default, link costs MUST be adjusted so no adjacency between FGL-safe switches costs more than 200,000. All FGL switches must also be connected to each other without passing through a VL switch. On mixed links, an FGL designated RBridge MUST appoint only FGL ports as forwarders for VLANs mapped to FGL.
sections.eli5: Some old mail carriers do not understand the new long stickers and might deliver the mail to the wrong house. So the new carriers route around the old ones, or refuse to hand them any long-sticker mail.

sections.title: IS-IS, ESADI and Registrations
sections.content:
FGL needs a few additions to TRILL's use of IS-IS. A switch announces that it is FGL-safe in its LSP. A new sub-TLV, called INT-LABEL in RFC 7176, lists interested labels the way the Interested VLANs sub-TLV lists VLANs. Three sub-TLVs, GLMAC-ADDR, GLIP-ADDR and GLIPV6-ADDR, play the role of the group-address sub-TLV for FGLs.

The ESADI protocol, which optionally shares MAC address attachment information inside TRILL Data packets, is extended so the FGL an ESADI packet applies to is given only in the packet's Inner.Label, never inside the ESADI payload.

The IEEE Registration Authority assigned Ethertype 0x893B for TRILL FGL, and IANA allocated capability flag 1 in the TRILL-VER sub-TLV to indicate that a switch is FGL-safe.
sections.eli5: The switches need a way to tell each other which sticker numbers they care about and whether they understand the new stickers, so the building's directory gets a few new lines.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC refers readers to RFC 6325 for general TRILL security and notes that sensitive data should use end-to-end encryption and authentication.

The specific danger is confusion between a packet with VL X and one with FGL (X.Y), or between either and a malformed frame. A VL switch that does not discard a packet with an unexpected value after the Inner.MacSA could egress it into VLAN X, violating the policy of keeping differently labeled data apart, or prune a multi-destination packet on the wrong basis so it fails to reach all recipients.

To avoid these problems, all TRILL switches MUST check the Ethertype immediately after the Inner.MacSA and, if they do not know it, either discard the frame or make no decisions based on data after it. FGL packets must also be kept away from VL switches as described in Section 5.1.
sections.eli5: The risk is a mail carrier misreading a label and putting a private letter in the wrong mailbox, so everyone has to check the first part of the label before doing anything else.

fields.name: Inner.Label High Part
fields.desc: 3-bit priority, 1-bit DEI, 12 label bits. Priority used across the campus.

fields.name: Ethertype
fields.desc: Must be 0x893B again, otherwise the packet is discarded.

fields.name: Inner.Label Low Part
fields.desc: 3-bit priority, 1-bit DEI, 12 label bits. Original priority restored on egress.
